o.text: Likely borrowed from Turkish bilim. By surface analysis, bil- (“to know”) + -im.
From Proto-Turkic *sīl- (“to wipe, rub”). Cognates include Turkish silmek, see there for more.

From Arabic دُنْيَوِيّ (dunyawiyy). By surface analysis, dünya (“world”) + -vi.
The shift from the sense mundane to secular is probably resulting from a semantic loan from Russian светский (svetskij).
Cognate with Uzbek dunyoviy.
From Arabic أَسْرَار (ʔasrār), broken plural of Arabic سِرّ (sirr).
Borrowed from Arabic مُهَاجَرَة (muhājara), verbal noun of هَاجَرَ (hājara).
Borrowed from Russian гидроаэродро́м (gidroaerodróm). By surface analysis, hidro- + aerodrom.
Borrowed from Russian гидрохимия (gidroximija). By surface analysis, hidro- + kimya.
